title: Serving Runtime — Consolidated Reference: architecture, scheduling, profiling, benchmarks, runbooks
author: Ava Thompson
content:
Purpose

This document consolidates the Serving Runtime team’s canonical reference for runtime architecture, kernel scheduling heuristics, profiling/playbook procedures, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, operational runbooks, and team wiki pointers. It is intended for engineers onboarding to serving-runtime, SREs who operate inference fleets, and performance engineers validating model performance across hardware.

Scope
- Architecture: logical components, data paths, and service boundaries.
- Kernel scheduling: policies, heuristics, and tunables.
- Profiling playbook: step-by-step profiling and root-cause workflows.
- Benchmarking suite: how to run, interpret, and extend benchmarks used for model onboarding.
- Release notes: summary of notable changes in the last two releases.
- Known issues: active issues and mitigations.
- Runtime runbooks: incident response flows for common alerts.
- Team wiki: ownership, contacts, and links to supporting docs.

1) High-level runtime architecture

Summary
The Serving Runtime is a high-throughput inference engine designed to serve sequence-generation and embedding workloads with low tail latency and cost-efficient batching. Primary production deployment is Redwood Dedicated and Hosted API. The runtime is deployed as a set of co-operating microservices on GPU nodes.

Core components
- frontdoor-proxy: TLS-terminating edge service that authenticates requests and enforces per-customer quotas.
- router: policy engine that routes requests to the appropriate model route and capacity tier (hosted/dedicated/private).
- scheduler (serve-scheduler): responsible for batching, kernel selection, and assignment to execution workers.
- execution-worker (serve-worker): GPU process that manages model weights, KV cache, and runs optimized kernels. Multiple workers run per GPU (one per MIG when applicable).
- kv-cache: in-process LRU prefix cache for recurring prefixes (also persisted to Redis for warm restarts).
- metrics-exporter: collects token-level latency, GPU utilization, batch size distribution, and per-route cost.
- model-store: artifact storage and metadata for model versions, quantization profiles, and kernel compatibility flags.

Data path (request flow)
1. Request arrives at frontdoor-proxy (auth + rate-limit).
2. Router selects route and model variant; applies routing policies (latency-first, cost-first, region).
3. Request enters serve-scheduler: scheduler attempts to coalesce into an existing batch or creates a new one based on batching window and deadlines.
4. When batch is ready, scheduler selects kernel and worker using kernel selector heuristics and dispatches execute command.
5. execution-worker performs KV cache lookup, runs forward kernels, and streams tokens back via router/frontdoor.
6. Metrics-exporter emits per-request and per-token metrics to metrics ingestion (Prometheus -> Cortex).

Design invariants
- Deterministic fallbacks: when preferred kernels or hardware are unavailable, scheduler chooses compatible alternatives guaranteeing functional equivalence (may degrade latency/cost).
- No single-request preemption: a running GPU kernel is allowed to finish; prioritization happens at batch scheduling boundaries.
- Observability-first: metrics and traces must cover each step (route selection, scheduling decision, kernel ID, worker ID).

2) Kernel scheduling: policies and heuristics

Goal
Minimize tail latency while maximizing GPU throughput and reducing per-token cost. Scheduling balances: batch formation latency, kernel throughput at expected sequence lengths, and KV/cache re-use benefits.

Primary heuristics
- deadline-based batching: each request has a soft deadline (default 25ms for low-latency tier, 100ms for default tier). Scheduler waits until either batch size or deadline is met.
- sequence-length bucketing: requests are grouped by estimated remaining length to reduce underutilized padding.
- kernel-cost-estimate scoring: scheduler keeps an internal table of kernel performance (tokens/sec, memory) per model-arch x device; when selecting kernel it scores candidates by weighted metric: score = alpha * predicted_tail_latency + beta * (1 / tokens_per_second) + gamma * memory_headroom_penalty.
- KV locality preference: prefer workers that already have warm KV cache for the requested model shard to avoid KV repopulation overhead (weight +10%).
- GPU-reservation for SLO-critical customers: some customers have pinned reservations on specific GPUs; scheduler enforces reservation constraints first.

Config knobs (defaults shown)
- batching_window_ms: "25"  # base waiting window for low-latency routes (ms)
- max_batch_size: "256"  # cap to prevent OOMs
- sequence_bucket_threshold: "8"  # bucket width in tokens
- kernel_selection_alpha: "0.6"
- kernel_selection_beta: "0.3"
- kernel_selection_gamma: "0.1"
- kv_locality_weight: "0.1"
- deadline_low_latency_ms: "25"
- deadline_default_ms: "100"

Example kernel selection table (excerpt)
| model_family | device | kernel_id | tokens/s | avg_95_latency_ms | memory_mb | quantized | notes |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| redwood-v1-7b | A100-80GB | ker_v1_fp16_opt | 42000 | 130 | 32000 | false | Best for long sequences >512 tokens |
| redwood-v1-7b | A100-80GB | ker_v1_q2_opt | 39000 | 140 | 16000 | true | 4-bit quantized: lower mem, small latency regress |
| llama2-13b | H100-94GB | ker_l2_h100_fused | 34000 | 120 | 44000 | false | fused attention kernels for H100 |

Note: the kernel table is updated by the benchmarking pipeline (see Benchmarking suite).

3) Profiling playbook (step-by-step)

When to run profiling
- Reproduced SLO regression in canary or prod.
- New kernel integration or compiler change.
- Significant model or quantization profile update.

Quick checklist
1. Reproduce workload with the profiling harness (use isolated staging cluster).
2. Capture end-to-end traces (trace-id present on metrics logs).
3. Collect GPU and host-level telemetry.
4. Run kernel-level profiling for the suspect time window.
5. Triangulate root cause and propose remediation (kernel config, batching changes, memory layout).

Commands and tools
- Start workload harness (k8s job):

```
kubectl apply -f ci/profiling/harness-job.yaml --namespace=profiling
```

- Tail traces (temporary trace token):
```
curl -H "X-Trace-Id: <TRACE_ID>" https://router.internal/route/<route_id>/stream
```

- GPU telemetry (prometheus queries):
```
# GPU utilization 1m avg for node-123
sum(avg_over_time(nvidia_gpu_utilization_percent[1m])) by (instance)
```

- Kernel-level profiling (NVIDIA Nsight CLI example):
```
nsys profile -o /tmp/profile.qdrep --trace=nvtx,cuda --capture-range=kernel --gpu-metrics-device=0 --duration=30s --attach-pid <serve-worker-pid>
nsys stats /tmp/profile.qdrep
```

- Lightweight sampling (perf + BPF):
```
perf record -F 200 -p <serve-worker-pid> -g -- sleep 30
perf script | flamegraph.pl > /tmp/flame.svg
```

Interpretation guide
- If kernel tokens/s is significantly below historical baseline for same kernel_id, check memory allocation patterns (OOM or fragmentation).
- High scheduler queue latency + small batch sizes indicates batching-window misconfiguration or increased request burstiness.
- Frequent worker VM restarts with warm KV miss rate > 30% -> investigate eviction thresholds or Redis persistence.

4) Benchmarking suite: running and extending

Purpose
The benchmarking pipeline validates kernels, quantization profiles, and deployment configurations across target device families. Results feed the kernel selection table and quantization recommendations.

Bench types
- synthetic-throughput: synthetic token streams at fixed concurrency and fixed sequence length to measure steady-state tokens/sec.
- latency-p95: single-request latency microbench using realistic prompts and early-stopping.
- real-workload-sampling: replay of production-sampled requests to measure end-to-end behavior incl. KV cache effects.

How to run (ad-hoc)
1. Checkout repo and build bench image:
```
make -C infra/bench images
```
2. Launch cluster (example uses bench-cluster):
```
utils/bench/launch_cluster --config infra/bench/bench-config.yaml --device a100-80
```
3. Run suite:
```
benchctl run --suite=latency-p95 --model=redwood-v1-7b --device=a100-80 --output=results/v1-7b-a100-202802
```
4. Upload results to results-bucket and trigger result-processor:
```
aws s3 cp results/v1-7b-a100-202802 s3://redwood-bench-results/2028/02/
curl -X POST https://ci.internal/bench/result-processor -d '{"path":"s3://redwood-bench-results/2028/02/v1-7b-a100"}'
```

Interpreting results
- Compare tokens/s and p95 against baseline CSV (baseline maintained in infra/bench/baselines.csv).
- If p95 regression > 15% or tokens/s drop > 10% for a production kernel, open PERF-XXXX ticket and notify serving-runtime slack channel (#serving-runtime-performance).

Extending the suite
- Add a new bench definition under infra/bench/suites/*.yaml and add docker image to CI build matrix (see infra/bench/README.md). Include model fingerprints and a quantization profile id.

5) Recent release notes (high-level)

Release: 2028-02-05 (v3.12.0)
- Added kernel_selection_alpha tuning exposed via /config API.
- New fused attention kernel for Llama2 on H100 (ker_l2_h100_fused).
- Reduced default batching_window_ms from 30 -> 25 for low-latency tier.
- Bench pipeline now stores per-kernel memory profiles.

Release: 2028-01-10 (v3.11.0)
- KV cache persisted to Redis during graceful shutdown to reduce cold-start misses.
- Added new metrics: serve_worker_batch_count and serve_worker_kv_hits.

6) Known issues (active)

- ISSUE-2154: H100 kernel oom during multi-model workload on 80GB host. Symptom: occasional OOM kill with long sequences > 1024 tokens. Mitigation: reduce max_batch_size to 128 for affected hosts; longer-term: patch kernel to reduce temporary buffer. Status: in_progress. Owner: Samuel Lee.

- ISSUE-2201: Sporadic p95 regressions after CUDA driver 12.3 upgrade. Symptom: 3-5% p95 increase on some kernels. Mitigation: pin driver to 12.2 on canary; rollback plan documented in infra/driver-rollback.md. Status: monitoring. Owner: Riya Patel.

- ISSUE-2278: KV eviction thrashing during heavy embed workloads. Symptom: KV hit rate drops below 60% for certain routes. Mitigation: increase kv_cache_size_mb for embed-heavy routes; add guardrails to scheduler to prefer locality. Status: mitigated. Owner: Kai Morgan.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational playbooks)

A. Alert: high serve_scheduler_queue_latency (> 50ms 5m rolling, SLO violation)
1. Pager to oncall SRE.
2. Check metrics dashboard: scheduler_queue_latency, batch_size_distribution, requests/sec.
3. If batch_size median < 4 and queue latency high: temporarily increase batching_window_ms by +10ms for affected routing group.
4. If GPU utilization < 60% but queue backlog exists: check for worker OOM or process restarts (k8s describe pod; check logs /var/log/serve-worker.log).
5. If widespread, roll forward to previous kernel or scale worker replicas for affected nodepool.
6. Create incident channel #incident-serve-scheduler and update status page.

B. Alert: worker OOMs (OOMKills > 5 in 10m)
1. Identify pods: kubectl -n runtime get pods --field-selector=status.phase=Failed -l app=serve-worker
2. Inspect pod events and memory usage; check dmesg for OOM killer.
3. Reduce max_batch_size for the nodepool: patch config map runtime/nodepool-<id>/config.yaml -> set max_batch_size: 128 and apply.
4. If immediate mitigation needed: cordon node and migrate.
5. After stabilization: open PERF ticket and schedule kernel memory investigation.

C. Alert: p95 regression for canary route
1. Run profiling playbook (see section 3).
2. Compare benchmark results for kernel_id in question.
3. If new kernel caused regression, roll back kernel via model-store to last-good kernel and re-run bench suite.

Primary owners

Useful internal links

Onboarding checklist (new engineers)
1. Read this consolidated reference.
2. Complete the bench runner tutorial: infra/bench/README.md.
3. Shadow an oncall rotation and run through a simulated incident (game-day).
4. Run one end-to-end bench and submit a bench result PR for review.

Appendix: example runtime config (yaml)

```
# runtime/nodepool-1/config.yaml
nodepool_id: "nodepool-1"
device_type: "a100-80"
max_batch_size: 256
batching_window_ms: 25
sequence_bucket_threshold: 8
kernel_selection_alpha: 0.6
kernel_selection_beta: 0.3
kernel_selection_gamma: 0.1
kv_cache_size_mb: 32768
reserved_for_customers: ["cust-1234","cust-2345"]
```

If you have questions or need escalation, ping #serving-runtime (Slack) or email serve-runtime@redwood.com.
